label: Variational Principles
notes: Open by reframing mechanics: instead of asking which force pushes a particle at each instant, we ask which whole trajectory a system selects between fixed endpoints. The action functional scores every candidate path, and nature picks the stationary one. This single idea unifies Newton, Lagrange, and Hamilton across the chapter.

label: Functionals and Variations
notes: Stress that a functional eats an entire curve and returns one number, unlike an ordinary function of finitely many variables. Introduce the admissible variation eta that vanishes at both endpoints, so the perturbed curve still connects the same boundary points. The parameter epsilon turns the search over curves into ordinary calculus.

label: The First Variation
notes: Walk through differentiating the action with respect to epsilon at zero. Integration by parts moves the derivative off eta-dot, and the boundary term dies because eta vanishes at the ends. What survives is an integral of eta against a bracket, and arbitrariness of eta forces that bracket to vanish pointwise.

label: Euler-Lagrange Equations
notes: State the Euler-Lagrange equation as the necessary condition for a stationary curve. Emphasize it is generally a second-order differential equation in q once the total time derivative is expanded. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations is the logical hinge that converts an integral identity into a pointwise equation.

label: Hamilton's Principle
notes: Introduce the Lagrangian as kinetic minus potential energy and define the action as its time integral. Hamilton's principle asserts that physical motion makes the action stationary, not necessarily minimal. Caution students that least action is traditional language; stationarity, including saddle behavior on long intervals, is the precise statement.

label: Equivalence to Newton
notes: Carry out the computation that the Euler-Lagrange equation for L equals T minus U reproduces mass times acceleration equals minus gradient of U. The momentum derivative gives the inertial term and the potential derivative gives the force. This is the proof that the variational and Newtonian formulations are the same physics.

label: Varied Paths Picture
notes: Use the diagram to make variation tangible: the bold curve is the true motion, the faint curves are competitors sharing both endpoints. The vertical gap between them is epsilon times eta. Action is stationary exactly when first-order changes in the path produce only second-order changes in the action value.

label: Legendre Transformation
notes: Define the conjugate momentum as the derivative of L with respect to velocity, then build the Hamiltonian as the Legendre transform of the Lagrangian. Geometrically the transform encodes a convex function by its tangent lines, trading slope for intercept. Convexity in velocity is what guarantees the transform is invertible.

label: Hamilton's Equations
notes: Show that rewriting the Euler-Lagrange equation in the new variables splits one second-order equation into two first-order equations. Phase space doubles the dimension but linearizes the bookkeeping. Point out the antisymmetric structure: q-dot reads off the p-derivative of H, while p-dot is minus the q-derivative.

label: Cyclic Coordinates
notes: A coordinate is cyclic when the Lagrangian does not depend on it explicitly, only on its velocity. Then the Euler-Lagrange equation says the conjugate momentum has zero time derivative, hence is conserved. Translational and rotational symmetries surface here as ignorable coordinates whose momenta are constants of motion.

label: Noether's Theorem
notes: Present the first look at Noether: a one-parameter family of transformations leaving the Lagrangian invariant produces a conserved quantity along solutions. The proof differentiates the invariance condition and uses the Euler-Lagrange equation to recognize a total time derivative. Symmetry and conservation become two faces of one statement.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tracing the logical chain: action functional, first variation, Euler-Lagrange, Hamilton's principle, Newton recovered, Legendre to Hamilton, and symmetry to conservation. Encourage students to run the notebook lab, perturb a trajectory, and watch the action stay stationary to first order while symmetry-protected momenta hold fixed.
